title: Nullable Value or Fallback
statement:
`int` cannot be `null` -- it is a value type, and a value type variable
always holds an actual value. `int?` (short for `System.Nullable<int>`)
adds exactly one more state on top: "an `int`, or nothing at all", which is
precisely the shape a sensor reading that has not arrived yet, or an
optional setting nobody configured, actually has.

## Your function

```
public static int ValueOrDefault(int? value, int fallback);
```

Return `value` if it holds one, or `fallback` if it does not.

## Watch out

- **`value.Value` throws if `value` is `null`.** It is legal, compiling
  code -- `int? x = null; int y = x.Value;` -- and it throws
  `InvalidOperationException` the moment it runs. This function exists
  specifically so a caller never has to reach for `.Value` (or check
  `.HasValue` by hand first) at all.
- **`??`, the null-coalescing operator, is the whole function.**
  `value ?? fallback` reads as "`value`, or `fallback` if `value` is
  `null`" -- which is exactly the specification above, word for word. A
  solution built out of an explicit `if (value.HasValue)` branch is not
  wrong, just longer than the language already offers to make it.
- `fallback` itself is a plain non-nullable `int` -- it is always a real
  value, never something that itself needs a further fallback.

tests.name: a present value is returned unchanged, fallback ignored
a present value of zero is not confused with absent
tests.description: 0 is a real value -- .HasValue is true for it, unlike for null.

tests.name: negative values round-trip through the nullable normally
